html:
A form of Chinese theatre that joins singing, speech, mime, acrobatics and stage combat. It took shape in Beijing in the late 1700s and 1800s, under the Qing dynasty, and came to be seen as China's national opera.

Its start is usually dated to 1790, when four troupes from Anhui province came to Beijing to perform for the 80th birthday of the Qianlong Emperor. They stayed, and over the next decades mixed their tunes with those of troupes from Hubei and other regions. The court, and above all the Empress Dowager Cixi, loved it.

The stage is nearly bare, and meaning is carried by set signs. Roles fall into fixed types: men, women, painted face warriors and clowns. Face paint colours show character, red for loyalty, white for cunning. For a long time all roles were played by men. The great female role actor Mei Lanfang took it on tours to Japan, the United States and the Soviet Union in the 1920s and 1930s. During the Cultural Revolution only a handful of model revolutionary operas were allowed.
